sm: The speaker, Marcos Eberlin, argues that life shows foresight, meaning solutions that anticipate problems in advance. His first example is the aquaporin, the water filter in cell membranes, whose passage matches the width of a water molecule so that only water enters. Because water normally carries protons along with it, an asparagine amino acid at the passage turns the water molecule ninety degrees, which he compares to cutting a wire so protons are blocked. He notes that the 2003 Nobel Prize went to the scientists who discovered how it works and asks what prize the designer deserves. His second example is the appendix, which he says hides beneficial gut bacteria during diarrhea, helps the immune system, and can now often be treated with antibiotics instead of surgery.

Eberlin goes quickly through more problem and solution pairs from his book. Ribosomes link amino acids in the right order to make proteins, kinesins act as nano robots that carry cargo along protein highways inside cells, and the Issus insect uses gears to make fast, synchronized jumps. He adds that hardening of the egg wall ensures only a single sperm fertilizes the egg, and that short-lived male moths have antennas able to detect a few molecules of a female's scent from kilometers away, far more sensitive than mass spectrometers. He concludes that irreducible complexity, information in life, fine tuning of the universe, and these examples of foresight, an ability unique to a mind, make him more confident that an intelligent mind made the universe and life.
